prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms confined at the magic wavelength have taken the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as a single-part prize to Katori and Ye. After round 1 I think the chair's central question has a physical answer. The 2005 comb prize gave us a way to count optical cycles, and the 2012 ion prize gave control of one isolated quantum system. The lattice clock is a different idea: choose the wavelength at which the light shift of the two clock states cancels, so that many atoms sit in a standing wave, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and are interrogated together. That brings both the statistics of an ensemble and the cleanliness of a trapped particle, and neither earlier prize contained it. The result has been reproduced and intercompared over optical fibre by laboratories in Japan, the USA, France, Germany, the UK and China, and the systematic corrections (magic wavelengths, blackbody shift, higher-order light shifts) rest on atomic-structure calculations that have been tested against experiment for years. That agreement between theory and experiment is the robustness I look for. The credit is Katori for the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye for the accuracy and stability frontier and for the many-body physics inside the lattice. The citation must be anchored on invention and realization, not on the record.
statement.case_against: The novelty objection has not gone away and I do not think it can be fully answered by argument. A committee that applies a strict standard of surprise about nature will find the Z2 topological insulator or the IceCube flux more striking than a better clock. Reasonable colleagues will call the lattice clock an outstanding refinement of recognised ground. The attribution is also a judgement: Lemonde, Takamoto, Boyd and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups made real contributions, and Ye's results depend on comb and laser-stabilisation technology and on a large JILA team. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so the payoff is still partly prospective. Finally, my own field is close to the magic-wavelength physics, so I may be too ready to see the idea as new.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B008 and argues that it is the clearest case of a simple general mechanism, with theory first and experiment second, confirmed independently by transport, ARPES and STM, and with unusually uniform agreement on the trio among the six members who ranked it highly.
responses.response: I agree that the Z2 mechanism is the most elegant idea on our list, and I ranked it second for exactly that reason. Where I part from him is the claim that agreement on the trio settles attribution. The six opening proposals agree because they copied the same obvious answer, but the HgTe proposal that made Molenkamp's experiment possible came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the three-dimensional generalisation from Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and Roy, with Hasan's experiments. A citation worded around Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is defensible, but it leaves out the person who told the experimenters where to look. On the 2016 prize, I agree with Eriksson that the Z2 classification is a distinct step, so I do not count it against B008 more than the 2005 and 2012 prizes count against B035. That is the same standard of adjacency for both, as the chair asks, and by that standard neither is disqualified. The difference between us is that the clock has a cleaner two-name credit.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B008 first as a new quantum state of matter and, in his reply to the chair's questions, is open to testing a B035 plus B008 pairing if a three-person ceiling can be made to work.
responses.response: I considered the pairing seriously. It cannot be done with the credits as proposed, because B008 needs three names and B035 needs two, which makes five, and cutting either is not honest. A pairing with Kane and Mele for the prediction alone, and Katori alone for the clock, would drop Molenkamp and Ye, and I would not defend that. I therefore keep a single-part prize. I also take his point that the first-principles band-structure calculations make the HgTe claim checkable. That is the quality I value, but it is also true of the lattice clock, where the shifts are calculated and then tested against independent clocks. If the committee prefers B008 I could support it, and I would then want the citation to name both the prediction and the first observation.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that lattice clocks are chiefly a gain in precision, whereas IceCube found something nature had not told us before, and he would resist trimming Karle without a decisive argument.
responses.response: I have thought about his distinction and I think it is partly right: a flux of astrophysical neutrinos was unexpected, and a better clock is not unexpected in that way. But precision is how fundamental physics advances. A clock at the 10^-18 level shows gravitational redshift across a millimetre, which a few years ago was out of reach, and it searches for drifting constants. I keep my question to him from round 1. If the committee cites the diffuse flux and the detector, and leaves the TXS and NGC 1068 associations aside, then the case is a measurement of a flux, and the credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA pioneers is exactly as hard as he admits. I defer to him on astroparticle judgement, so I place B023 as an alternative and not above the clock, but I cannot argue that its credit is cleaner.

responses.point: Olsson supports B035 but asks whether Ye's credit is the original idea or the later accuracy record, and says the citation must be anchored on invention and realization.
responses.response: I agree with the question and I think it has an honest answer: Ye's credit is not the original idea, which is Katori's, but taking it to the accuracy and stability frontier and showing the many-body physics of a lattice clock. That is a real invention step and a realization step, and I would accept wording that makes the division explicit. I therefore keep 'invention and realization' and the magic wavelength in the citation. If the committee wants that division stated more strongly I would not object, but I would not rebuild the credit around Lemonde or Takamoto, because I cannot weigh priority dates without an expert report.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moves B035 ahead of his own opening choice, B023, because it combines strong merit with broad support, and he asks whether the redefinition of the second should bear on timing.
responses.response: I agree with him that support counts should not replace judgement, and I have tried to keep my preference on the science. On timing, I do not think the formal redefinition of the second is a reason to wait or to act now. The prize should rest on the invention and the 10^-18 results, which are already established, and not on a decision by the metrology bodies. I also note that his adjacency disclosure for IceCube argues for caution on B023 in discussion, and that Johansson's disclosure for circuit QED does the same, which is part of why I do not move to B004 even though I ranked it third on the physics.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is a distinct invention after the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. I judge it is, but I cannot prove it.

Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Boyd and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups have priority claims that should change the two-name credit. An expert report on the early strontium and ytterbium demonstrations would settle this better than discussion.
Whether B008 would prove the stronger choice if the committee regards novelty about nature as the decisive standard and accepts the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang.
I have not independently verified specific record accuracy values and rely on my knowledge of the literature.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I work in atomic structure theory, which is close to the physics of the magic wavelength, and I collaborate with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate), who is not a candidate. I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye, nor with the other shortlisted candidates. I do not request recusal on B035, but I leave it to the committee to decide whether the field closeness should be recorded.
